intro: The Ride of the Valkyries, an orchestral excerpt from Wagner’s Die Walküre, WWV 86B, has rushing strings and a loping brass tune. This Edison disc from 1921 lasts four minutes.

sections.label: Intro · Upward string runs under woodwind
sections.mNote: Upward string runs pass beneath the woodwind.

sections.label: A · The riding tune in the brass
sections.mNote: The broad tune sounds above the quick accompaniment.

sections.label: B · Gallop accompaniment continues
sections.mNote: The accompaniment keeps its three-beat rhythm.

sections.label: A′ · Brass calls over rapid strings
sections.mNote: Brass hold long notes above faster string figures.

sections.label: Coda · End of the ride
sections.mNote: The orchestral ride ends with the end of the disc.

cues.title: Opening string figures in 9/8
cues.text: The string groups play short upward runs in alternation, with woodwind notes held above them. Wagner writes in 9/8, three beats to the bar with each beat divided into three. The brass tune that follows is in the same metre.
cues.evidence: Wagner, Der Ritt der Walküren, Schott concert full score, plate 22159, pp. 2–3: 9/8, upward string figures and woodwind entries. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4a/IMSLP1006817-PMLP4725-ROTV2.pdf. The precise edition and cuts used on the Edison disc are unidentified.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Edison recording, 1921
cues.text: The American Symphony Orchestra recorded the Ride for Edison in 1921. It was released in December 1921 on Diamond Disc 80638-R.
cues.evidence: Thomas Edison National Historical Park recording catalogue: recorded 1921, released December 1921; Edison Diamond Disc 80638-R, matrix 7846-B-1-6, object EDIS 41877. https://www.nps.gov/edis/learn/photosmultimedia/classical-instrumental.htm.

cues.title: Dotted riding tune in the brass
cues.text: The riding tune stretches dotted notes across the busy accompaniment. The strings keep up their rapid figures under the brass melody’s long-short rhythm.
cues.evidence: Schott concert full score, pp. 3–6, dotted riding figure and quicker string accompaniment. This note describes the recurring theme, without assigning an entrance to this timestamp.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Act III, scene 1
cues.text: At the opening of Act III, the Valkyries gather on a mountain with the dead heroes they have collected for Wotan. Their calls to one another, from rock to rock, cross the orchestral gallop. This recording is orchestral and leaves out the voices.
cues.evidence: Wagner, Die Walküre, Act III, scene 1, stage directions and Valkyries’ dialogue; synopsis at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Walk%C3%BCre. Dramatic context: the voices are absent from this orchestral disc.

cues.title: Brünnhilde’s arrival with Sieglinde
cues.text: In Act III, scene 1, Brünnhilde arrives carrying Sieglinde, a living woman she has rescued against Wotan’s command. Her sisters refuse to help her. The ride leads directly into this scene.
cues.evidence: Wagner, Die Walküre, Act III, scene 1; synopsis at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Walk%C3%BCre. This is the surrounding opera’s action, not a synchronisation of the shortened recording with Brünnhilde’s entrance.

composer.epithet: Composer who placed the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth, hidden from the audience.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no real success. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons playing against the storm music in the strings. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to get his music staged.

He grew up in the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. He heard Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies, and in 1831 he took counterpoint lessons from Theodor Weinlig. Posts followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen was not performed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, failed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
